summary: Deep technical session on on-prem air-gapped deployment requirements. Covered artifact delivery options, offline licensing and key handling, GPU driver and CUDA compatibility, and runtime performance tradeoffs (KV cache, batching, quantization). Action items agreed: Redwood to deliver offline bundle and benchmarks; Aurelia to provide inventory and prompt sets. Plan for 2-day pilot workshop pending inventory confirmation.
topics: KV cache behavior and warm-up strategies
continuous batching and latency vs throughput tradeoffs
quantization impacts on quality and perf
transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm lena from redwood, joining me is marco our se. we have about an hour, is that still okay?
[00:12] Raj Patel: yes, thanks lena. we blocked this time to go deep on the air-gapped install questions. Aisha and maya will jump in for security and ops.
[00:20] Aisha Rahman: hi, quick note — we're recording for notes only, fine.
[00:27] Marco Diaz: great, i'll kick off with an overview of the artifacts and what we typically ship for an on-prem air-gapped bundle. then we can go into drivers, licensing, and perf.
[00:34] Marco Diaz: so typical bundle: model weights (or pointers to local tarballs), runtime binaries (redwood runtime, kernel modules if needed), our docker images as tarballs, and an offline license token tool. everything is checksummed (sha256) and we provide a README with install order. we can deliver via secure file transfer or encrypted HDD depending on you.
[00:52] Samir Gupta: for us encrypted HDDs are preferable, data center has strict control. how does the offline license tool work? we can't have outbound calls.
[00:59] Marco Diaz: right, for air-gapped we use a signed license token. redwood generates a license payload tied to your org id and hardware fingerprint (optional). you run the token activation CLI that validates signatures offline against the public key shipped with the bundle. no outbound required.
[01:16] Maya Chen: hardware fingerprinting is sensitive for us. can we avoid shipping any device-identifying bits?
[01:21] Lena Park: yes, we have two modes: hardware-locked tokens (recommended for high-security environments) or org-scoped tokens that are activated on a specific admin node and can be rotated manually. we can document both flows.
[01:33] Aisha Rahman: do you integrate with our KMS / HSM? our policy requires keys be stored in HSM for long-term secrets.
[01:40] Marco Diaz: we support HSM-backed key storage for customer-managed private deployments. activation can store the license in your HSM via our CLI plugin; otherwise the token is stored encrypted on disk. we'll include the plugin in the offline bundle.
[01:53] Raj Patel: switching to drivers: we're running RHEL 8.6 on nodes, mostly A100 and a couple of L40s. we have mixed kernels 5.10 and 5.15. CUDA versions are currently 11.8 on some machines. what are your requirements?
[02:07] Marco Diaz: for the latest runtime we support CUDA 11.7+ and 12.x; specific kernel modules depend on the vendor drivers. A100 is supported; L40 we have validated but we'll need the exact driver builds. we'll produce a compatibility matrix in the bundle.
[02:21] Samir Gupta: i worry about proprietary GPU driver licensing — our ops team needs the full offline install procedure for the NVIDIA drivers. do you provide proprietary drivers?
[02:29] Marco Diaz: we do not redistribute NVIDIA's proprietary drivers. we provide the install automation and a list of exact driver packages (rpm/deb) and checksums that your procurement can fetch under your license from the vendor and then we include them in the HDD if you want. Alternatively, procurement can provide us with the driver package and we can sign/verify it into our bundle but we don't ship vendor binaries by default.
[02:47] Maya Chen: that matches our procurement constraints. for validation, are there kernel module patches or DKMS steps?
[02:53] Marco Diaz: mostly standard nvidia-dkms or rpm installs. we have some helper scripts to white-list modules and set persistence mode. if you need patched kernels (rare) we'll call that out.
[03:02] Lena Park: moving to runtime perf: marco, can you explain kv cache warm-up and batching implications in an air-gapped setup?
[03:09] Marco Diaz: sure. KV cache is stored in-memory per session; warm-up cost depends on prompt prefix reuse. in production we recommend prefix caching on a separate persistent cache tier if you have long-lived sessions — in air-gapped installs that's typically an in-cluster memory cache or shared redis (we provide a redis-compatible shim if you can't run external services).
[03:30] Maya Chen: we prefer no additional services initially; can we rely on local node cache?
[03:34] Marco Diaz: yes. local node KV cache works fine but you lose cross-node reusing. that means higher token compute and higher latency for cold starts. for throughput-sensitive workloads we suggest sticky routing (pin session to same node) plus a small in-memory LRU prefix store.
[03:49] Raj Patel: how big is the memory overhead per session for KV cache on, say, a 8k context?
[03:55] Marco Diaz: ballpark: for 8k tokens in a decoder-only model KV takes roughly 2-3x the model hidden size in bytes, roughly 4-8 GB for large models depending on quantization and dtype. we'll provide exact numbers for your model in the benchmark report.
[04:10] Samir Gupta: speaking of quantization — we plan to run int8 for cost — how does quantization affect KV cache size and latency?
[04:16] Marco Diaz: quantization reduces memory footprint (kv storage smaller) and often improves throughput but may increase latency slightly on some ops due to dequantize/requantize steps. with our runtime we push quantized kernels to reduce those costs; in practice int8 gives 1.6–2.5x throughput improvement with small quality delta on many models. we'll run quality checks against your eval set.
[04:37] Aisha Rahman: any concerns about model determinism after quantizing? we need reproducible outputs for audit scopes.
[04:43] Marco Diaz: quantization can introduce non-determinism, yes. we recommend keeping a small evaluation set and threshold-based quality monitoring. we can also offer per-route quantization profiles: keep sensitive routes in fp16/float and batch queries for cost.
[04:58] Lena Park: latency targets? what did you say earlier, maya?
[05:02] Maya Chen: we want p95 < 300ms for short intents (<=128 tokens) and throughput of ~100 requests/s for bulk APIs.
[05:10] Marco Diaz: p95 300ms is achievable on dedicated A100 pools for small prompts with sticky routing and warm caches. main levers: reduce batch size (to keep latency), increase concurrency, CPU preprocess offload, and quantization. if you can accept p95 500ms we can push higher throughput per GPU.
[05:28] Raj Patel: what about batching policies — we have bursty traffic; does your runtime support dynamic batching?
[05:34] Marco Diaz: yes, continuous batching with deadline-based flush (max batch latency) is supported. you can set target SLOs per-route and runtime will adapt batch windows. we also have on-device batch packing for short sequences so GPU utilization increases without blowing up latency.
[05:49] Samir Gupta: are there any NIC or RDMA requirements? our data center topology is 100GbE with RoCE.
[05:56] Marco Diaz: RoCE is supported; for multi-GPU cross-node KV sync we can use gRPC over RDMA or fallback to TCP. we'll include configuration templates for your fabric.
[06:07] Maya Chen: do you recommend multi-instance sharding or tensor parallel across GPUs for our workloads?
[06:13] Marco Diaz: depends on model size. for <70B we tend to prefer model sharding + pipelining or replicated smaller micro-batches. for big models, a combination of tensor parallel and pipeline parallel is optimal. We'll recommend configuration after we see the exact model and throughput targets.
[06:28] Raj Patel: on the license side, what's the rotation/renewal experience for air-gapped tokens?
[06:34] Marco Diaz: tokens are time-limited. renewal can be done offline: we generate a new token signed with our private key and deliver via the same offline channel. for safety you can rotate keys locally in the HSM and have per-installation key expiry policies.
[06:46] Aisha Rahman: audit logs — we need local audit trails of who activated what and when.
[06:51] Marco Diaz: activation is logged locally. the CLI writes an audit record including installer user, timestamp, and token fingerprint. logs can be exported to your SIEM.
[06:59] Raj Patel: benchmark plan?
[07:02] Marco Diaz: we'll run three benchmark passes: cold-cache single-node, warm-cache single-node, and multi-node throughput. metrics: p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec, GPU utl, memory usage, and kv-hit ratio. we'll include raw traces and flame graphs.
[07:19] Maya Chen: can you run an initial benchmark with our sample prompt set in staging? we can provide logs and sample data.
[07:24] Marco Diaz: yes, please share prompts; we'll run in our staging configured to mirror your kernel/driver versions as closely as possible and return results. for final validation we prefer running same tests in your environment — that'll be part of the pilot.
[07:36] Lena Park: i'll follow up with the procurement template and a checklist for HDD delivery and checksums.
[07:42] Raj Patel: on the artifact details, can you list exact files in the bundle?
[07:47] Marco Diaz: yes — bundle contents include: runtime tarball, model weight tarball (or manifest), docker image tars, license-cli binary, activation public key, install scripts, driver rpm/deb manifests, kernel-module helpers, config templates, and the offline bundle README with sha256. we'll attach a compatibility matrix.
[08:07] Samir Gupta: when you say "manifest" — is that a signed manifest?
[08:10] Marco Diaz: yes, manifests are signed; we use layered signing for the model and runtime artifacts. signature verification is part of the activation flow.
[08:18] Maya Chen: any documented rollback procedures if an install fails?
[08:22] Marco Diaz: yes, the installer creates checkpoints and you can revert to previous docker image layers and restore previous license tokens. we'll document the steps and test them in the pilot.
[08:33] Aisha Rahman: security question — do any components phone home for telemetry?
[08:37] Lena Park: by default, private/on-prem installs have telemetry off. we only enable if the customer opts in, and telemetry can be forwarded to a customer endpoint inside the network.
[08:46] Aisha Rahman: good. also, we need all crypto algorithms and key lengths documented for compliance.
[08:50] Marco Diaz: we'll include a crypto appendix: RSA-4096 signing for token signatures, AES-256 GCM for on-disk secrets, and TLS1.3 for any optional connect paths.
[08:59] Raj Patel: let's talk about the driver installation steps quickly — what's the recommended order?
[09:03] Marco Diaz: typical order: (1) kernel updates if needed, (2) install vendor driver rpms (NVIDIA/CUDA), (3) reboot to activate drivers, (4) install docker/runtime and set nvidia-container-toolkit, (5) deploy redwood runtime images, (6) run activation CLI. We'll provide idempotent scripts.
[09:22] Samir Gupta: reboots are painful — can we do driver install on maintenance window only.
[09:26] Marco Diaz: absolutely, scripts are safe to run in maintenance windows; we also provide dry-run output to validate steps.
[09:33] Maya Chen: performance question — you mentioned dequantize overhead earlier; can you give numbers for int8 vs fp16 latency on small prompts?
[09:40] Marco Diaz: rough numbers from our internal tests on A100: fp16 p95 for 128-token prompt ~ 180-220ms; int8 p95 ~ 200-260ms but tokens/sec increases. exact numbers depend on model and kernel ops; we'll run your eval set and share a table.
[09:58] Raj Patel: about KV eviction — how do you avoid cache blow-up with many concurrent sessions?
[10:03] Marco Diaz: we implement adaptive eviction with LRU per-shard and a global memory cap. sessions that exceed memory thresholds get their prefix stored compressed to disk or drop older prefixes. We can tune thresholds per node.
[10:16] Samir Gupta: does disk compression add unacceptable latency?
[10:19] Marco Diaz: there is a latency hit but it's applied to less-frequent prefixes. hot paths remain memory-resident. we only compress cold prefixes.
[10:29] Maya Chen: any gotchas with mixed CUDA versions across nodes? we sometimes have staggered upgrades.
[10:34] Marco Diaz: mixed CUDA is tricky for shared deployments. we recommend homogeneous runtime images per cluster. If unavoidable, we run routing policies so requests route to compatible nodes. We'll provide helm charts to express per-node capabilities.
[10:50] Raj Patel: provisioning — how big is the disk footprint for the bundle?
[10:54] Marco Diaz: depends on models; the runtime + tooling is ~2-4GB. Model weights vary — for a 13B model compressed weights ~5-10GB int8; larger models scale accordingly. We can provide a per-model manifest with exact sizes.
[11:08] Maya Chen: about monitoring — can redwood console be deployed entirely on-prem?
[11:12] Marco Diaz: yes, the console can be deployed in your VPC. by default we ship a control-plane agent that talks only to the local console; nothing needs to leave your network.
[11:23] Aisha Rahman: outstanding compliance docs we need: SOC2 report, pen-test summary, architecture diagrams.
[11:29] Lena Park: we'll attach SOC2 summary and our latest pen-test high-level findings. detailed reports can be handled under NDA.
[11:36] Raj Patel: okay next steps recap?
[11:39] Lena Park: marco will prepare the offline bundle and the manifest; i'll send the procurement template and pilot scope; aurelia to share GPU inventory and prompt set; we schedule pilot week once inventory confirmed.
[11:50] Raj Patel: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[11:54] Maya Chen: thanks, logging this into our ticketing system.
[11:57] Marco Diaz: thanks all, talk soon.
